content.title: Circular Track Problem: Distance vs Displacement
content.problem_statement: An athlete runs along a circular track of radius seven metres. Find the distance travelled and the magnitude of displacement when the athlete completes (a) half a revolution, and (b) one full revolution. Take pi as twenty-two over seven.

steps.narration: For half a revolution, the athlete runs along exactly half the circle. The distance covered is half the circumference, pi times the radius, which with pi as twenty-two over seven and radius seven metres works out to exactly twenty-two metres.
But the displacement after half a revolution is just the straight line across the circle, the diameter. That's twice the radius, so two times seven, which is fourteen metres.
Now for a full revolution, the athlete runs all the way around the circle once. The distance is the full circumference, two pi R, which comes out to forty-four metres.
But notice, after one full revolution, the athlete is back exactly where they started. So even though the distance covered is a huge forty-four metres, the displacement is zero.
steps.display_text: Full revolution: back to the start

content.final_answer: For half a revolution, the distance is twenty-two metres and the displacement is fourteen metres. For a full revolution, the distance is forty-four metres, but the displacement is zero.
content.final_answer_latex: \text{Half: } d=22\text{ m}, s=14\text{ m} \quad \text{Full: } d=44\text{ m}, s=0

metadata.description:
One of the most important distance vs displacement problems: an athlete running on a circular track. We find distance and displacement for both half a revolution and a full revolution, showing exactly why displacement can be zero even after running a long distance. A must-know result for Class 9 Physics Motion and a frequent JEE/NEET concept check. Subscribe for a full chapter-by-chapter walkthrough of Class 9-12 Physics and Math!
